Learning Objectives
Explain the importance of proper patient positioning during orthopaedic surgery.
Identify the most common patient positions used during orthopaedic surgery and review
special considerations for each position.
Review the importance of padding bony prominences to prevent pressure ulcers,
compartment syndrome, and other pressure-related injuries.
Recognize the challenges in proper positioning of patients with obesity.
Introduction
Proper surgical positioning mitigates patient morbidity from pressure-related injuries, nerve-
related injuries, and eye injuries.
Proper positioning requires knowledge of patient positions, vigilance, and teamwork.


Introduction
Although often overlooked, proper patient positioning is important for all orthopaedic
surgical procedures.1 The goal of patient positioning is to facilitate the procedure and
minimize any risk of patient injury. Improper patient positioning may lead to substantial
morbidity, including pressure-related injuries, nerve-related injuries, and eye injuries.1-
11 In addition, improper patient positioning may lead to potential malpractice litigation,
accounting for 16% of all malpractice lawsuits in a single anesthesiology claims
database.2 Prevention of these injuries requires vigilance and teamwork.
Different surgical procedures require varied patient positioning. Therefore, orthopaedic
residents must understand various patient positions. Patients with obesity present
additional challenges in patient positioning; general principles should be further
emphasized in those patients.12 The goal of this lesson is to review the most common
patient positions used in orthopaedic surgery, focusing on critical tips for each position.
General Tips and Recommendations
Follow the basic principles of positioning for all procedures to minimize nerve traction and
pressure-related injuries: place the head and spine in a neutral position, pad all bony
prominences, avoid shoulder abduction and elbow flexion beyond 90°, and place the forearm
in a supinated or neutral position.
Ensure the selected surgical table meets all the needs of the procedure (fluoroscopy,
radiography, hand table) and can safely handle the weight of the patient. 

General Tips and Recommendations
The basic principles of positioning should be followed for all surgical procedures. To
prevent pressure-related injuries, pad all bony prominences (eg, fibular head, elbows,
iliac crests) and ensure the sheets under the patient are free from wrinkles or
creases.1 To minimize cervical spinal cord traction, place the head and spine in a neutral,

nonrotated position.1 To minimize traction on the brachial plexus, avoid abduction of
the shoulders beyond 90°.1 To avoid traction on the ulnar nerve, prevent elbow flexion
beyond 90° and place the forearm in a supinated or neutral rotation.1 During normal
sleep, some movement is normal to prevent nerve stretching.
11 This movement is not
possible in patients who are anesthetized; therefore, positioning is crucial.
11
Surgical table selection should facilitate the needs of the surgical procedure, including
access for fluoroscopy or radiography or the addition of a hand table if necessary.
Ensure the area of interest is accessible for fluoroscopy. For example, a standard
surgical table with a central post works well if fluoroscopy of the extremities is
necessary; however, fluoroscopy of the pelvis or spine would require a surgical table that
does not have a central post, such as a Jackson table. Check the standards of the surgical
table to ensure it can handle the weight of the patient; special attention to positioning
and padding is required in patients with obesity.11
Supine Position
The supine position is a versatile and widely used surgical position, particularly in patients with
multiple fractures (Figure 1).
Back pain and peripheral nerve injury are common complications with the supine position but
can be mitigated by following basic principles.

Figure 1 Illustration shows a patient in the supine position.

Supine Position
The supine position is a versatile, widely used surgical position in numerous orthopaedic
subspecialty procedures, including fracture fixation, arthroplasty, foot and ankle, upper
extremity, hand, and spine procedures.1 The supine position is the preferred position in
any emergency case.1 The head, neck, and spine remain in a neutral position. Tissues
overlying bony prominences, such as the heels and sacrum, are padded to prevent
pressure-induced soft-tissue ischemia.11 The upper extremities can be abducted or
adducted in various combinations depending on the procedure. For all patients, the
arms should be placed in a neutral position in no more than 90° of abduction to
minimize ulnar nerve pressure and brachial plexus traction, respectively.1 The patient is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Surgical Positioning and Monitoring
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003004
4/20

secured to the surgical table with the use of a safety belt that is placed approximately 2
inches above the knees. The hip can be bumped and elevated to better access the lateral
aspect of the leg or the thigh. The supine position may be advantageous in patients with
multiple fractures because of the decreased need for repositioning and because it allows
for sequential or simultaneous procedures.1
Common complications associated with the supine position include back pain and
peripheral nerve injury.11 Back pain is caused by relaxation of the back muscles with
general anesthesia, which results in loss of normal spine curvature.11 Patients with
extensive kyphosis or scoliosis may require extra padding or slight flexion at the hip and
knee.11 Ulnar neuropathy and brachial plexus injury are the most common peripheral
nerve injuries associated with the supine position.11 Maintenance of the head in a
neutral position and maintenance of arm abduction of less than 90° minimizes the risk
of brachial plexus traction10,11 (Figure 2). Ensuring the forearm is well padded and in a
supinated or neutral position prevents ulnar nerve injury.10

Figure 2 Illustration of a patient in the supine position shows that the brachial plexus is
vulnerable to stretch and compression. Arm abduction past 90° causes the head of the
humerus to stretch the plexus. Shoulder braces and head rotation also may cause
compression.
Lateral Decubitus Position
The dependent upper and lower extremities, the eye, and the ear are at risk of injury with the
lateral decubitus position.
Protect the dependent axilla via proper positioning of the chest roll caudal to the axilla.
The risk of complications is increased with the use of traction for shoulder arthroscopy. 

Lateral Decubitus Position
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Surgical Positioning and Monitoring
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003004
6/20

Lateral decubitus positioning is common for hip arthroplasty, lower extremity fracture
fixation, shoulder arthroscopy, and elbow fracture fixation1,13 (Figures 3 and 4). The
patient is rolled onto the nonsurgical extremity with the surgical extremity upward. The
patient is secured with the use of an inflatable bean bag, peg board with gel foam
padding and pegs, or a specialized padded hip table. The torso must be balanced and
supported with the use of padding.11 The head should be maintained in a neutral
position1 (Figure 5). The dependent arm should be secured outward on a padded stand
or on pillows perpendicular to the torso.11 The nondependent arm should be
supported.11 Neither arm should be abducted more than 90°, and both arms should be
kept in neutral rotation.1 The axilla should be clear without any pressure, and an axillary
roll should be placed under the axilla on the chest wall; this prevents extension and
traction/compression on the brachial plexus11 (Figure 6). Padding should be placed on
all bony prominences, including the fibular head, lateral leg, and lateral malleolus of the
down leg, as well as between the knees to minimize excessive pressure.11 The trunk and
the down leg should be safely secured to the surgical table. Patients may be flexed in the
lateral position to attain better access to the retroperitoneum.11
Figure 3 Anterior view illustration shows a patient in the lateral decubitus position.

Figure 4 Posterior view illustration shows a patient in the lateral decubitus position.
Lateral decubitus positioning is associated with many of the same complications as
supine positioning.1 The dependent ear and eye are at risk for injury and should be
assessed regularly throughout the surgical procedure.11 In an anesthesia case series of
eye injuries that occurred during non-ocular surgical procedures, lateral positioning was
an independent risk factor for eye injury, most commonly corneal abrasion.14 The
dependent brachial plexus and the axillary neurovasculature are at risk of
compression.11 Proper placement of a chest roll caudal to the axilla and ensuring the
dependent axilla is clear will protect the shoulder from the force of gravity.11
Compression may cause vascular compression and venous outflow obstruction.11
Decreased pulse and low pulse oximetry may be early signs of compromised blood
flow.11 Brachial plexus palsy, traction-related soft-tissue injury, digital nerve
compression, ischemic injury, and an increased risk of neurovascular injury have been
associated with the use of traction during shoulder arthroscopy in the lateral decubitus
position.1 Therefore, the weight of traction used to distract the surgically managed
extremity should not exceed 20 lb (9 kg).1

Beach-Chair Position
Head positioning is crucial in the beach-chair position to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion or
neuropraxia of the cervical nerves.

Beach-Chair Position
The beach-chair position is most commonly used for clavicular, shoulder, and humeral
surgical procedures1,15,16 (Figure 7). The patient is first positioned supine on a table
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Surgical Positioning and Monitoring
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003004
10/20

with mobile joints to sit the patient upright. A head holder often is used; the head should
be secured in place with the use of padded straps in a neutral rotation or slightly rotated
to the contralateral side to facilitate access to the surgical field.1 The patient’s torso is
moved to the edge of the bed toward the surgical extremity and secured in place with
the use of padded straps.1 The patient’s buttocks should be placed in the break of the
bed so the patient does not slide distally.1 A pillow placed under the knees prevents
extension at the hips and can help prevent the patient from sliding distally.1 The bed is
then brought into the beach-chair position by moving the bed into a slight
Trendelenburg position; the back of the table is raised 50° to 60°, and the knees are
flexed approximately 20°.1 The contralateral arm can be secured across the torso with
the use of padding and secured in place; alternatively, it can rest at the patient’s side on
a padded stand. The surgical extremity can be rested on a sterile stand or a specialized
arm-positioning device.
Care should be taken so that the head is in a slightly flexed position, especially in
patients with considerable cervical spondylosis.16 Excess rotation of the head may
occlude vertebral artery blood flow and cause neurapraxia of the cervical cutaneous
nerves.1,16 Cerebral hypoperfusion is a concern if the patient’s head is elevated above
the heart; regional anesthesia compared with general anesthesia and ensuring an
adequate heart rate and blood pressure throughout the procedure may prevent
cerebral ischemic events.1,16

Prone Position
Ensure proper head positioning and safe transfer of patients in the prone position.
Prone positioning is associated with the greatest risk among surgical positions, especially for
perioperative vision loss.
Ensure weight is properly distributed to the bony pelvis and that the abdomen and genitalia
are free from compression.
The prone position is commonly used for posterior spine procedures. 

Prone Position
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Surgical Positioning and Monitoring
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003004
12/20

Common surgical procedures in which the prone position is used include spine
procedures, acetabular fracture fixation, and some lower extremity trauma
procedures.11 Anesthetized patients should be slowly rolled into a prone position. Great
care should be taken to ensure that the head is in a neutral position; several devices,
including head pins, head holders, and commercially available pillows, can facilitate this,
depending on the surgical procedure.11 Ensure that no pressure is on the eyes, ensure
that the airway is secure, and ensure that weight is placed on the bony facial
prominences.11 The prone position is a risk factor for perioperative visual loss.11 The
arms can be placed at the patient’s side with the thumbs upward or on padded arm
boards with the shoulders abducted no more than 90° and the elbows flexed no more
than 90°. The elbows should be well padded. Padded rolls should be placed under the
chest, abdomen, and iliac crests.1 The hips and knees are slightly flexed, with padding
and/or pillows supporting them.11 Breasts should be placed medially to the torso
supports, and genitalia should be free of compression.11 The abdomen should hang
freely to prevent increased intra-abdominal or intrathoracic pressure1 (Figure 8).
The prone position may be the most difficult and highest-risk position with regard to
complications.1,17 For posterior spine surgery, low venous pressure is desirable to
minimize blood loss and improve exposure.11 Increased intra-abdominal pressure
compresses the vena cava, resulting in increased venous return that may be diverted to
the valve-less vertebral venous system.1 Selecting a surgical table that minimizes
abdominal restriction may mitigate this risk.1 For acetabular fracture fixation, the hip
often is extended, and the knee is flexed to relax the sciatic nerve. The bed often is
placed into the reverse Trendelenburg position to decrease facial edema.1 Other
complications associated with the prone position include airway edema, eye injury,
pressure injury, and inadvertent loss of the endotracheal tube.11
Perioperative visual loss is a rare complication of non-ocular surgery, frequently
secondary to ischemic optic neuropathy and retinal artery occlusion.11 Although rare,
occurring in 1 of 60,000 to 1 of 125,000 patients, spine fusion is associated with a higher
incidence compared with other surgical procedures (3 of 10,000 to 9 of 10,000).11
Surgical time greater than 6 hours and blood loss greater than 1 L are risk factors for
perioperative visual loss secondary to ischemic optic neuropathy.11

Traction Table
Always attempt to use the least amount of traction necessary.
Traction tables are commonly used in the management of femur fractures.

Traction Table
Several types of traction tables exist; however, the general principles for patient
positioning are similar.1 Common surgical procedures in which a traction table is used
include femoral fracture fixation, anterior total hip arthroplasty, and hip arthroscopy.
Anesthetized patients are moved to the well-padded traction table; a padded perineal
post is placed, and the patient is moved down with the perineum on the post. The feet
should be well padded and placed into the traction boots, ensuring they are fully
secured. The contralateral lower extremity can be placed in the lithotomy position,
extended and abducted, or abducted to allow access for fluoroscopy to obtain direct
lateral images; in any of these positions, care should be taken not to overly abduct,
extend, or flex the contralateral lower extremity. The contralateral upper extremity

9/4/26, 9:44 AM
AAOS | Surgical Positioning and Monitoring
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003004
14/20

typically can be padded and secured at the patient’s side or abducted on an arm board,
avoiding shoulder abduction of more than 90°; depending on the procedure, the surgical
side upper extremity can be placed at the patient’s side or secured across the patient’s
chest for intramedullary femoral nail placement (Figure 9). 
Case reports of compartment syndrome of the contralateral lower extremity have been
described with the hemilithotomy position because of increased compartment
pressures.18,19 Excess traction or an improperly padded perineal post may result in
pudendal nerve injury or perineal pressure injury.20,21 Muscle relaxants should be used
to avoid excessive traction forces necessary to complete the procedure.1 Periodic
release and/or use of the least amount of traction necessary to complete the procedure
is ideal to avoid traction-related complications.1
Figure 9 Illustration shows positioning of a patient on a traction table.
Patients With Obesity

Patients with obesity pose numerous challenges to perioperative management (Video 1).
Ensure the selected surgical table can withstand the patient’s weight and follow basic
principles of surgical positioning, with additional attention to skin folds and appropriate
padding.
Video 1 Dunahoe JA, Fernando N: The Obesity Epidemic: Implications for Orthopedics and
Current Trends in Management [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/22996__Videos. Accessed May
4, 2022.

Patients With Obesity
Positioning of patients with obesity is more challenging. Not only is airway management
and anesthesia induction more difficult in patients with obesity, the risk of compartment
syndrome and pressure-related complications as a result of positioning is increased.
Table-weight specifications should be assessed to ensure the table selected is
appropriate for the size of the patient.1,12 Additional attention to skin folds and

16/20

appropriate padding is necessary. Focus on padding and proper positioning should be
increased in these patients.1,12
Summary/Outcomes

Summary/Outcomes
Proper patient positioning is an important aspect of all orthopaedic surgical procedures.
Improper patient positioning may lead to considerable patient morbidity, including
pressure-related injuries and nerve-related injuries. In addition, improper patient
positioning may lead to potential malpractice litigation, accounting for 16% of all
malpractice lawsuits in an anesthesiology claims database.2 Different surgical
procedures require varied patient positions, requiring orthopaedic surgical residents to
understand various patient positions. Patients with obesity presents additional
challenges in positioning; general principles should be further emphasized in those
patients. Surgeons, anesthesiologists, and operating room staff must work together to
achieve patient safety and desired surgical exposure.
